tldr: By integrating multi-array plantar pressure sensors into the soles of a humanoid robot and providing direct feedback on pressure distribution and temporal changes, the authors propose a reinforcement learning framework that enables stable walking across steps, slopes, and even unseen foam mats and gravel roads without falling.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of Tac4Loco. Simulated and real-world pressure signals are preprocessed into a shared ordinal discrete representation, encoded via a dual-branch spatial-temporal network, trained with an asymmetric actor-critic architecture, and deployed zero-shot onto the real Unitree G1 humanoid robot.
overview:
For humanoid robots to walk stably on rough terrain, they must accurately understand how their feet interact with the ground. However, conventional 'blind locomotion' relying solely on joint information (proprioception) can only infer plantar support indirectly, causing delayed reactions when stepping on an edge or slipping. On the other hand, camera-based visual perception is useful for predicting terrain before touchdown, but it cannot observe the actual load and support distribution in real time once contact is made.

To address this challenge, the authors propose 'Tac4Loco', a tactile-perceptive locomotion framework that directly incorporates signals from multi-array plantar pressure insoles into the control policy. Its core innovation is quantizing pressure values into 'ordinal load ranks (discrete bins)', resolving sensor-to-sensor inconsistencies typical of low-cost sensors and bridging the simulation-to-reality gap. In addition, the authors developed a dual-branch encoder that separately processes the spatial pressure topology across the foot sole and its temporal evolution since touchdown.

Experiments were conducted in both simulation and the real world using the Unitree G1 humanoid. Beyond handling slopes and stepping over obstacles, the robot maintained stable locomotion without falling on challenging surfaces never encountered during training—such as compliant foam platforms that deform under load and granular gravel roads—demonstrating the power of direct plantar tactile feedback.
contributions: Proposed Tac4Loco, a humanoid locomotion framework that utilizes the spatial distribution and temporal dynamics of multi-array plantar pressure sensors as direct post-touchdown feedback.
Designed a topology-preserving ordinal quantization method that maps simulated and physical sensor signals into a shared ordinal scale to bridge the Sim-to-Real gap.
Developed a dual-branch plantar pressure encoder that separately extracts motion-conditioned spatial features and recent temporal load trends.
Demonstrated zero-shot deployment on the real Unitree G1 robot across inclined, partial, and changing supports, as well as unseen compliant foam and unstructured gravel terrains.

sections.heading: Why Humanoids Need Tactile Sense Under Their Feet
sections.summary: When humanoids walk on rough terrains designed for humans, plantar support conditions are constantly unstable. Because conventional joint proprioception and visual perception cannot capture the realized support state at the instant of touchdown, an approach that directly exploits plantar pressure distributions is required.
sections.details:
When a humanoid robot traverses outdoor or uneven environments, foot-ground contact conditions are fraught with uncertainty. Foot placement errors, ground slope, or stepping on the edge of an obstacle can lead to partial foot contact or severe load imbalances. Because these plantar support conditions shift dynamically with the gait cycle and body motion, they directly impact locomotion stability.

Existing locomotion policies rely primarily on proprioception from joint encoders and IMUs, or exteroceptive perception from depth cameras. However, proprioception can only infer ground support indirectly, leading to inherent reaction delays. Meanwhile, vision helps predict terrain before touchdown, but cannot verify in real time whether reliable support has actually been established once the foot hits the ground.

While some prior works incorporated plantar contact sensors, most reduced the rich tactile signal to a binary contact flag, total ground reaction force, or the Center of Pressure (CoP). These low-dimensional statistics cannot distinguish between full planar support and precarious two-point support across the heel and toe, since both scenarios can yield similar total forces and CoP locations. To overcome this limitation, the authors developed Tac4Loco, which preserves both the spatial load topology and the temporal pressure dynamics for direct locomotion control.

sections.heading: Bridging 'Blind' Joint Sensing and 'Superficial' Vision
sections.summary: Humanoid locomotion research has largely split into 'blind' proprioceptive control and 'vision-based' terrain-aware control. However, the former suffers from delayed reactions while the latter cannot observe post-touchdown contact dynamics, creating a clear need for direct plantar tactile sensing.
sections.details:
Related work broadly falls into two categories. The first is proprioceptive (blind) locomotion relying solely on joint sensors and IMUs. Researchers have employed domain randomization, curriculum learning, and history-based network architectures to improve robustness against disturbances. While immune to sensor latencies and visual occlusions, these policies suffer from an inherent delay: they only detect contact events after the torso shakes and loads are transmitted up to the joints.

The second category is exteroception-based (visual) locomotion using depth images or elevation maps. This allows proactive foot placement planning. However, it remains vulnerable to camera blind spots, processing latencies, and calibration drifts. Crucially, it cannot capture post-touchdown physical dynamics, such as soil shifting or foam compressing underfoot.

While foot tactile and pressure sensors have attracted attention, prior studies mainly utilized them for support polygon reconstruction in model-based control or as auxiliary loss terms in motion-imitation learning. Leveraging dense multi-array pressure sensor data as a direct feedback signal in reinforcement learning for humanoid locomotion has remained largely unexplored.

sections.heading: Inside Tac4Loco: A Dual-Branch Encoder for Spatial-Temporal Tactile Signals
sections.summary: The proposed framework quantizes plantar forces into an ordinal scale to absorb physical sensor variance, then extracts features via dual spatial and temporal branches. This is combined with kinematic terrain inclination estimates and trained using an asymmetric actor-critic architecture.
sections.details:
The Tac4Loco pipeline is carefully designed to capture foot contact states on rough terrain and ensure smooth simulation-to-reality transfer.

- Problem Formulation (III-A): Formulated as a discrete-time Markov Decision Process. The policy (actor) observation $o_t$ consists of standard proprioception $b_t$ (joint states and IMU), the current discrete pressure map $P_t$, the historical pressure and motion sequence $H_t$, and a terrain inclination feature $e_t$. The output $a_t \in \mathbb{R}^{29}$ represents residual joint position targets relative to a default standing stance.

- Pressure Quantization (III-B): The real robot uses 60-element FSR (Force Sensitive Resistor) insoles on each foot. Because FSR sensors exhibit significant element-to-element variability, measuring exact forces in Newtons is unreliable. Recognizing that relative load distribution patterns matter far more for stability than absolute forces, the authors introduced an ordinal quantization mapping $Q(F)$. After calibrating real readings against simulated normal forces using a quadratic function, values are mapped into 31 non-uniform discrete bins (0 to 30; 50g steps below 1000g, 100g steps from 1000g to 2000g). This shared ordinal representation effectively bridges the Sim-to-Real gap.

- Observation Construction (III-C): The quantized values are mapped onto a 2D spatial grid corresponding to sensor geometry, forming $P_t = [P_t^L, P_t^R]$. For the temporal history $H_t$, the sole is divided into 8 regions to extract a 21-dimensional summary descriptor $\phi(P_t)$ (regional load ratios, CoP shifts, etc.), concatenated with motion data into a 37-dimensional packet. It uses a 'dense-near, sparse-far' sampling strategy spanning 8 steps (3 consecutive recent frames and 5 sparsely sampled past frames).

- Terrain Inclination Estimation (III-D): Foot orientations $\theta_t^L, \theta_t^R$ are derived via forward kinematics. However, kinematic angles are meaningless when a foot is in mid-air or in partial contact. Thus, a contact confidence score $c_t$ is computed from the number and spatial spread of active pressure units. The slope estimate is updated only when firm contact is detected, decaying otherwise.

- Dual-Branch Encoder (III-E): The spatial branch tokens the pressure map via a CNN, then applies cross-attention using the robot's current motion state and gait phase as the Query. Because identical pressure patterns mean different things when moving forward versus stopping, this adaptively highlights relevant contact regions based on motion context. The temporal branch processes the 8-step history through a 1D temporal CNN, extracting the latest step, temporal average, and trend features before MLP compression.

- Training Setup (III-F): Policies are trained with PPO in an asymmetric actor-critic setup. The critic receives privileged information including true simulation velocities, contact forces, and local elevation maps. Alongside velocity tracking and stability rewards, a 'Plantar Support Alignment Reward' is introduced to align the foot sole normal with the ground reaction force vector, encouraging the robot to plant its feet securely.

sections.heading: From Simulation to Unseen Foam and Gravel: Putting Sole Tactility to the Test
sections.summary: In simulation, the framework significantly outperformed baselines on steep slopes, random steps, and V-shaped trenches. On the real Unitree G1, it demonstrated zero-shot locomotion across unseen compliant foam platforms and unstructured gravel roads.
sections.details:
Evaluations were conducted in simulation (MJLab) and on the real Unitree G1 robot, comparing Tac4Loco against an official proprioceptive-only baseline (Proprio-only) without pressure feedback.

- Simulation Evaluation (IV-B): Evaluated on flat ground, rolling hills (15 cm height variation), 15- and 20-degree slopes, random step fields (up to 15 cm step heights), and V-shaped trenches (0 to 25 degrees). While Proprio-only achieved survival rates of only 22.0% on slopes and 71.7% on random steps, Tac4Loco surged to 77.9% and 96.5%, respectively. It achieved 100% survival on flat ground, hills, and V-trenches. Drift angle away from the command direction was substantially reduced, and step length increased markedly: +33.2% on steps, +87.2% on slopes, and +82.9% on V-trenches, showing that the robot steps forward confidently without stumbling.

- Ablation Studies (IV-C): Removing the terrain inclination estimate ($e_t$) degraded velocity tracking on undulating terrain and lowered survival on slopes. Removing the pressure encoder increased lateral drift and reduced survival in V-trenches. This demonstrates that slope estimation handles continuous inclines, whereas the tactile encoder is vital for handling partial contacts and unexpected step edges.

- Real-World Deployment (IV-D): The simulation-trained policy was transferred zero-shot to the physical Unitree G1. In structured challenges—such as stepping down from a 9-degree ramp, traverse-walking across slopes, transitioning over a 15-degree uphill to 9-degree downhill peak, and crossing V-trenches—Proprio-only frequently caught its toes and fell or drifted down the slope, whereas Tac4Loco achieved high completion rates. Furthermore, the robot was tested on difficult unstructured terrains absent from training: compliant foam mats and gravel roads. When stepping onto the thick foam, the ground deformed locally underfoot; Tac4Loco immediately sensed the load shift and adjusted its center of mass to maintain balance. On the loose gravel road, it maintained stable locomotion for 5 minutes of continuous walking without a single fall.

sections.heading: Looking Forward: Towards Integrating Tactile and Visual Sensing
sections.summary: Representing multi-array plantar pressure across space and time dramatically enhances humanoid adaptability on complex terrains. Future work will look toward combining pre-touch visual foresight with post-touch tactile verification for multimodal locomotion.
sections.details:
This paper introduced Tac4Loco, a humanoid locomotion framework that leverages multi-array plantar pressure sensing as direct post-touchdown feedback. By resolving the Sim-to-Real gap with ordinal quantization, decoupling spatial and temporal features with a dual-branch encoder, and estimating terrain inclination modulated by contact confidence, the policy achieved remarkable walking stability in both simulation and real-world trials.

Real-world tests highlighted that plantar tactility serves as an essential line of defense against severe disturbances where joint sensors alone fail—such as partial foot placement on sharp step edges, compliant ground depression on soft foam, and shifting loose gravel.

For future work, the authors plan to integrate tactile feedback with exteroceptive visual sensing. Fusing visual foresight (anticipating terrain and selecting footholds before touchdown) with tactile reactivity (correcting loads immediately upon contact) will pave the way toward agile and robust all-terrain humanoid locomotion.

takeaways: Sensor discrepancies and Sim-to-Real gaps in low-cost FSR insoles can be effectively mitigated by quantizing forces into relative, ordinal discrete bins rather than relying on absolute readings.

Instead of compressing foot pressure into a single total force vector or CoP, separately encoding spatial contact topology and temporal load history dramatically improves adaptability to partial foot contacts and uneven loads.
Incorporating direct plantar tactile feedback enables zero-shot generalization to compliant foam and granular gravel surfaces that are notoriously difficult to model accurately in physics simulators.
limitations: Without exteroceptive vision, the robot cannot anticipate upcoming obstacles before foot contact, making it unable to preemptively avoid excessively tall obstacles or drop-offs.
The long-term physical durability of FSR insoles, including drift and increased hysteresis from extended real-world walking, has not yet been fully characterized.

The pressure sensor update rate is capped at 50 Hz, leaving it an open question whether the system can support highly dynamic gaits—such as high-speed running or jumping—where ground contact phases are extremely brief.
